# The datasets {#sec-data}

Day 1's datasets are simulated by `scripts/make_data.R`, from seed 2025. Run
`Rscript scripts/make_data.R` from the project root to regenerate all of them;
`data/PROVENANCE.txt` records when and with which R version. Days 2 to 6 add
three files that are not simulated here: a synthetic diabetes dataset shipped
with `mlbench`, and two small clinical teaching files used in the preprocessing
exercises. All five are described below.

Simulation is deliberate for Day 1, for three reasons. The generating process is known, so
every diagnostic question has a checkable answer. No information governance
approval is needed, so the files can live in a public repository. And the
defects are the ones we chose, so they can be taught.

## `los_data.csv` — the training world

1000 admissions. Used in Exercises 1.2 and 1.3.

| Column | Meaning | Generating process |
|---|---|---|
| `Age` | years | Normal(60, 15), truncated below at 18, **not truncated above** |
| `Severity` | severity score, 1–10 | Normal(5.4, 2.07), clipped to [1, 10] |
| `LOS` | length of stay, days | $-8.5 + 0.94\,\text{Age} + 3.37\,\text{Severity} + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 4.3)$ |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,30,56]"}

**Known defects, retained on purpose.**

- The maximum age is just over 109, and 26 patients are aged 90 or more. Nothing
  truncates the upper tail, exactly as in extracts
  where a default or mistyped date of birth survives into the warehouse.
- Typical LOS is about 66 days, which is wrong for acute medicine by an order of
  magnitude.
- `LOS` is symmetric. Real length of stay is strongly right-skewed. This is the
  single most recognisable difference between this file and a real one.
- Severity piles up at exactly 1 and 10 because the draw is clipped, not
  bounded: 2.0% of rows sit at 1 and 1.6% at 10.

Both of the first two are the subject of Exercise 1.2, Task 1.

These parameters match the `los_data.csv` distributed in earlier years of the
module, so answers stated as ranges are unaffected by which copy a student has.

## `extract_A.csv`, `extract_B.csv`, `extract_C.csv` — the later extracts

400 admissions each. Used in Exercise 1.3. Students are told only that they are
monthly extracts taken after the model went live, and must diagnose what
changed. The mechanisms are in `scripts/make_data.R` and in the instructor
chapter.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Publishing note
`scripts/make_data.R` contains the answer to Exercise 1.3. If you publish the
student site from the same repository, either exclude `scripts/` from the
published output or accept that a determined student can read the key. Nothing
else in the booklet gives it away.
:::

## `los_data_skewed.csv` — the realistic variant

1000 admissions, same predictors, but LOS is drawn from a Gamma distribution
with a multiplicative mean, $\mathbb{E}[\text{LOS}] = \exp(0.15 + 0.012\,\text{Age} + 0.17\,\text{Severity})$,
shape 2. Median around four days, with a long right tail. Not used on Day 1;
it exists for the sessions on metrics and on generalised linear models, where
the difference between a symmetric and a skewed outcome changes the answer.

## `birthweight.csv` — the transfer task

600 pregnancies. `bpd` (biparietal diameter, mm) and `ad` (abdominal diameter,
mm) predict `bw` (birth weight, g) through
$-1700 + 30\,\text{bpd} + 25\,\text{ad} + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 250)$.
Units and magnitudes are plausible; the numbers are invented. Used in Exercise
1.2 Task 4 so that students rerun the pipeline on columns whose names bear no
resemblance to the ones they just used.

## `diabetes.csv` — the case study for Days 2 to 6 {#sec-data-diabetes}

768 adults, nine columns, exported from `mlbench`'s `SynthDiabetes` by
`scripts/make_data.R`. Every value is synthetic and no row corresponds to a real
person.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pregnant` | number of times pregnant |
| `glucose` | plasma glucose concentration, glucose tolerance test |
| `pressure` | diastolic blood pressure, mm Hg |
| `triceps` | triceps skin fold thickness, mm |
| `insulin` | 2-hour serum insulin, mu U/ml |
| `mass` | body mass index |
| `pedigree` | diabetes pedigree function |
| `age` | years |
| `diabetes` | `pos` or `neg` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[18,82]"}

**Known defect, retained on purpose.** Zeros appear where zero is
physiologically impossible: 52.7% of `insulin` values, 32.7% of `triceps`, 4.6%
of `pressure`, 1.7% of `mass` and 0.7% of `glucose`. They are missing values
written as zeros, and because they are numerically valid, every summary
statistic and every model will quietly use them. Finding them is the first task
of Day 2, and they are what makes the imputation and leakage exercises bite.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why this is synthetic, and why that is worth five minutes of class
These exercises were originally written against `PimaIndiansDiabetes`: data on
diabetes in Akimel O'odham ("Pima") women, collected by the US National
Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, which reached the UCI
Machine Learning Repository in the late 1980s and became one of the most-used
teaching datasets in the world.

Both UCI and `mlbench` have since withdrawn it. The `mlbench` changelog for
version 2.1-10 records the removal, and the documentation for the replacement
states that the data "had apparently been included without informed consent" in
those repositories, and that distribution ceased once it became clear the data
"had most likely been shared illicitly".

Copies remain on third-party mirrors, and nothing technical prevents their use.
The reason this booklet does not use them is that a teaching repository is a
publisher like any other. It is also a point worth making to the cohort
directly: consent does not expire because a file is convenient, a dataset's
ubiquity is not evidence that it was lawfully obtained, and "everyone uses it"
is the sentence that kept it in circulation for thirty years.

`SynthDiabetes` was created by Matthias Templ to mimic the data analysed by
Smith et al. (1988). It has the same size, the same columns and the same
defects, so the exercises are unchanged; only the values differ.
:::

## `longisland_heart.csv` — missingness to diagnose

200 patients, 14 columns, used in the Day 2 missing-data exercise. Each of the
13 predictors has exactly 20 missing values, and 150 of the 200 rows are
incomplete in at least one column — a pattern regular enough that students can
work out it was injected rather than observed, which is itself the point of the
first task.

Two things to say out loud when you use it. The outcome, `diagnosis of heart
disease`, has five levels rather than two. And the clinical variables are not in
clinical units: `trestbps` runs from 1 to 41 and `chol` from 1 to 100, so they
have been recoded or binned at some earlier point by someone who did not write
it down. That is an ordinary and instructive state for a teaching extract to be
in.

## `bupa.csv` — skewed variables to transform

345 patients, seven columns of liver-related blood tests (`mcv`,
`alkalinephosphotase`, `alamine`, `aspartate`, `gammaGlut`), plus `drinks` and a
`selector` field. Complete, with no missing values. Used in the Day 2
transformation exercise because `gammaGlut` and `alamine` are strongly
right-skewed, which is what makes a log transformation visibly do something.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A caution worth passing on
`selector` is often treated as a disease label in tutorials using this file. It
is not one: it was the field the original depositors used to split the data into
two sets. It splits this copy 200 / 145, and mean daily drinks are 3.39 and 3.54
in the two groups — an arbitrary partition, not a diagnosis. Any exercise that
predicts it is predicting the split. This booklet uses the file only for
transformation, where the label is irrelevant: `alamine`, `gammaGlut` and
`aspartate` have skewness 3.1, 2.9 and 2.3, which is what makes a log
transformation visibly do something.
:::

## Using real data instead

Any of these can be swapped for a real dataset, and the booklet's structure
survives it, but two things change and should be said out loud when you do it.
The known answer disappears, so the self-checks that compare against a key
(`check_shift_answers()`) no longer apply; and the defects become the ones the
extract happens to have rather than the ones the exercise needs. Teaching
diagnosis first on data with a known answer, then on real data, is the order
that works.
